name: Amami Brown Frog
description:
Brown frog family, genus Rana. *Rana kobai*

Grows to about 3.2-4.6 cm. Breeds from November through January. Lives in forests
and along rivers from lowlands to mountains. Becomes active on humid or rainy days,
and gathers around small ponds and spring-fed pools during the breeding season.
Individuals can also be seen along forest roads. Slender-bodied and reddish brown,
it calls with a sharp "kyok-kyok" note.

name: Amami Green Tree Frog
description:
Tree frog family (Rhacophoridae), genus Zhangixalus. *Zhangixalus amamiensis*

Grows to about 4.5-7.7 cm. Breeds from late December through around May. Found
from lowlands to mountains, in forests around ponds, rice paddies, and other still
water. It calls vigorously on humid or rainy days and lays white, foam-covered egg
masses on branches overhead or in streamside vegetation. Even when calling loudly,
it is very hard to spot. Larger than Hallowell's tree frog, which makes the two
easier to tell apart.

name: Amami Tip-nosed Frog
description:
Brown frog family, genus Odorrana. *Odorrana amamiensis*

Grows to about 5.6-10.1 cm. Breeds from October through May. Lives around
mountain streams. Slender with good posture, and once you get an eye for it, it
can be recognized even from a distance. Its coloring is rich and varies between
individuals. Designated a Natural Monument in Kagoshima Prefecture, so capturing
or transferring it — including its eggs — is prohibited. Many come out onto
forest roads when it rains, so drive carefully.

name: Amami Spiny Newt
description:
Newt family (Salamandridae), genus Echinotriton. *Echinotriton raffaellii*

Grows to about 14-20 cm in total length. Breeds from around January through
April. Endemic to Amami Oshima, Uke-jima, and Tokunoshima, it lives around
forests and farmland. It becomes active on warm winter days, and during the
breeding season lays eggs under fallen leaves near water. It has a rugged,
blackish-brown body, with orange tints on its rib-tip projections and the ends
of its limbs.

name: Amami Ishikawa's Frog
description:
Brown frog family, genus Odorrana. *Odorrana splendida*

Grows to about 7.4-13.7 cm. Breeds from late February through around June. Lives
along the gentle headwater streams of mountain areas. Said to be Japan's most
beautiful frog, it is designated a Natural Monument and a Nationally Rare Wild
Species in Kagoshima Prefecture, and capturing or transferring it — including
its eggs — is prohibited. In some spots near higher-elevation streams, its call
can be heard after dark, and at certain locations it can even be seen in summer
when it rains.

name: Amami Sword-tailed Newt
description:
Newt family, genus Cynops. *Cynops ensicauda ensicauda*

Males reach about 14 cm and females about 18 cm in total length. Found on Amami
Oshima, Uke-jima, Kakeromajima, Yoro-jima, and other nearby islands, it breeds
in ponds, rice paddies,
and gentle stretches of streams. After September most individuals leave the
water, and around December, during the breeding season, large numbers can be
observed at the water's edge. It has a black body with yellow or orange spots,
and individual variation is considerable. Okinawa is home to the related
Okinawa sword-tailed newt.

name: Hallowell's Tree Frog
description:
Tree frog family, genus Hyla. *Hyla hallowellii*

Grows to about 3-4 cm. Breeds from March through June. Lives in lowland forests,
thickets, and farmland, and lays eggs in rice paddies and other still water. It
becomes active on humid days and rainy nights, and during the breeding season
forms large chorus gatherings near rice paddies. It perches a little way up, such
as on the tips of branches, and even when calling loudly is hard to spot. Solid
green and very beautiful. Its call resembles that of the Japanese tree frog.

name: Okinawa Rice Frog
description:
Narrow-mouthed frog family, genus Microhyla. *Microhyla okinavensis*

Grows to about 2.2-3.2 cm. Breeds year-round (mainly March through July). Found
in a wide range of habitats from coastal lowlands to mountains, including forest
edges, grasslands, and around houses. Becomes active on humid or rainy days. Its
head is small and its legs are thick, giving it a triangular shape when viewed
from above. Japan's smallest frog, but it calls with a surprisingly loud voice.

name: Otton Frog
description:
Brown frog family, genus Babina. *Babina subaspera*

Grows to about 9-14 cm. Breeds from April through October. Lives mainly in
mountainous areas, but can also be seen in farmland and parks. It becomes active
on humid or rainy days and often comes out onto roads. Males grow larger, making
this Japan's biggest frog aside from the introduced American bullfrog. It has
five toes with a sharp spur on what corresponds to the thumb, thought to be used
by males when fighting each other or during amplexus. Designated a Natural
Monument and a Nationally Rare Wild Species in Kagoshima Prefecture, capturing
or transferring it — including its eggs — is prohibited. It is very large and
impressive, and easy to spot when it comes out onto a road. Its name is said to
come from its call.

name: Ryukyu Kajika Frog
description:
Tree frog family, genus Buergeria. *Buergeria japonica*

Grows to about 2.5-4 cm. Breeds from April through October. Adaptable to
habitats ranging from mountain streams to puddles in built-up areas, it is the
most commonly seen frog on Amami Oshima. It calls especially vigorously on
humid or rainy days. Males are a beautiful yellow, and their call is beautiful
too.

name: Red-bellied Long-legged Riffle Beetle
description:
Riffle beetle family, genus Stenelmis. *Stenelmis hisamatsui* M. Satô, 1960

A small aquatic beetle found in the Amami and Okinawa island groups and Guam.
Riffle beetles live mainly in clean streams; both larvae and adults spend their
lives in the water, growing to about 5mm at most, and the family is watched as
an indicator of clean rivers. The detailed ecology of this species itself is
still largely unknown.

name: Amami Broadbody Riffle Beetle
description:
Riffle beetle family, genus Dryopomorphus. *Dryopomorphus amami* Yoshitomi & M. Satô, 2005

An endemic species found only on Amami Oshima, described in 2005. The genus
Dryopomorphus also includes a widespread relative found on Honshu, Shikoku,
and Kyushu along with a smaller species, plus another species endemic to the
Osumi Islands. Riffle beetles are mainly small aquatic beetles living in clean
streams, but the detailed ecology of this species itself is still largely
unknown.

name: Amami Micro Water Boatman
description:
Pygmy water boatman family, genus Micronecta. *Micronecta japonica* Chen, 1960

A tiny aquatic true bug about 1mm long. Endemic to Japan, it is found in the Nansei Islands (Amami Oshima and Tokunoshima). Several related species are known within the same genus, including the more widespread Micronecta guttata, found from Hokkaido to Kyushu. It normally burrows into sand or fallen leaves, and swims away quickly when startled.

name: Amami Groove Riffle Beetle
description:
Riffle beetle family, genus Ordobrevia. *Ordobrevia amamiensis amamiensis* (Nomura, 1957)

A small aquatic beetle found on Amami Oshima (nominate subspecies). The population on Okinawa Island and Iheya Island is distinguished as a separate subspecies, the Okinawa groove riffle beetle (*O. a. okinawana*), and an introduced population is also known from Guam. Riffle beetles mainly live in
clean streams, but the detailed ecology of this species itself is still
largely unknown.

name: Amami Swimming Broad-shouldered Water Strider
description:
Broad-shouldered water strider family, genus Xiphovelia. *Xiphovelia curvifemur* Esaki & Miyamoto, 1959

A small broad-shouldered water strider found across the Nansei Islands, on Amami Oshima, Tokunoshima, and Okinawa Island. The closely related species Xiphovelia japonica favors gravel and bedrock along the shorelines of forest-ringed valley ponds, and has been confirmed to overwinter as eggs on floating plant debris or shoreline gravel, but the specific ecology of this species itself is still poorly understood. It should also be noted that the closely related Xiphovelia japonica is listed as Vulnerable (VU) on the Ministry of the Environment's Red List, whereas that designation concerns a different species and should not be confused with this one; this species itself is not listed on the Red List.

name: Amami Ridged Minute Moss Beetle
description:
Minute moss beetle family, genus Ochthebius. *Ochthebius amami* Yoshitomi & M.Satô, 2001

A tiny aquatic beetle described as a new species from an individual collected by chance on Amami Oshima in spring 1997, belonging to the minute moss beetle family (a different family from the "gamushi" water scavenger beetles despite the similar Japanese name). About 1.9-2.3mm long. Found on Amami Oshima and Okinawa Island, it lives in relatively open sections of mountain streams, though it is not very abundant. Habitat degradation from river development and bank reinforcement work is a concern, and it was newly listed as Near Threatened (NT) in the 2010 revision of the Ministry of the Environment's Red List.

name: Amami Clam Water Scavenger Beetle
description:
Water scavenger beetle family, genus Laccobius. *Laccobius satoi* Gentili, 1989

A small water scavenger beetle endemic to Japan, found in Amami Oshima and Tokunoshima. Several closely related species exist within the genus Laccobius in Japan, including L. fragilis and L. nakanei, and telling them apart requires examining the genitalia. Detailed records of its body length and ecology are scarce, and much remains unknown.

name: Amami Sidegroove Riffle Beetle
description:
Riffle beetle family, genus Leptelmis. *Leptelmis torikaii* Kamite, Yoshitomi & Hayashi, 2017

Endemic to Amami Oshima, a species described as recently as 2017. Its form
differs from other species in the same genus found on mainland Japan and
Taiwan, while the shape of its genitalia, among other features, closely
resembles a species distributed in southern China, indicating a close
relationship. It is regarded as an example of a relict endemic species: its
ancestral species is thought to have once been widespread across the Eurasian
continent, and after Amami Oshima became isolated, related populations
elsewhere died out, leaving only this species surviving. Riffle beetles are
mainly small aquatic beetles living in clean streams, but the detailed ecology
of this species itself is still largely unknown.

name: Toad Bug
description:
Toad bug family, genus Nerthra. *Nerthra macrothorax* (Montrouzier, 1855)

The only species of toad bug family found in Japan, about 1cm long, with a broad, flattened body. It has no ocelli and is distinguished by its thick, sickle-shaped front legs. Its Japanese name, Ashibuto-memizumushi, literally means "thick-legged water bug," but despite that name it does not live underwater in ponds; rather, it is a semi-terrestrial ambush predator active at night on sandy beaches (from the shoreline to the coastal forest), preying on pill bugs and woodlice, and overwintering as an adult. It is widely distributed from southern Kyushu through the Nansei Islands to the Ogasawara Islands, and is not endemic to Amami Oshima alone.

name: Brown Micro Water Strider
description:
Broad-shouldered water strider family, genus Microvelia. *Microvelia japonica*
Esaki & Miyamoto, 1955

A small aquatic insect about 1.5-2.1mm long. Found on Honshu (west of
Fukushima Prefecture), Shikoku, and Kyushu, and in the Ryukyu Islands from
Kikaijima to Okinawa Island. Commonly seen in dim pools beside small streams
and in the shade of rocks, where it preys on small insects that fall onto the
water's surface.

name: Notched Pygmy Backswimmer
description:
Pygmy backswimmer family, genus Heterotrephes. *Heterotrephes admorsus* Esaki & Miyamoto, 1959

The only species of the pygmy backswimmer family found in Japan, with a small, hemispherical body about 2.5-3mm long. Like the water boatman-relative backswimmers, it swims upside down. Known only from Amami Oshima and Tokunoshima, it is endemic to the Amami Islands, and lives in slow-flowing rivers, in spots where plant roots hang down from the bank into the water. It is listed as Vulnerable (VU) on the Ministry of the Environment's insect Red List.

name: Two-spotted Minute Diving Beetle
description:
Diving beetle family, genus Allopachria. *Allopachria bimaculata* (M.Satô, 1972)

A tiny diving beetle said to bear two spots on its elytra, as its species name (meaning "two-spotted") suggests. It is said to be distinguished from closely related species by its smaller body and the incomplete microreticulation on its head. It is found across the Nansei Islands, from the Tokara Islands through the Amami island group to Okinawa Island, and is listed as Near Threatened (NT) on the Ministry of the Environment's insect Red List. Primary sources on its detailed ecology and morphology are scarce.

name: Iriomote Micro Water Strider
description:
Broad-shouldered water strider family, genus Microvelia.
*Microvelia iriomotensis* Miyamoto, 1964

A small aquatic insect about 1.7-1.9mm long. Found in the Ryukyu Islands
(from the Amami group to the Yaeyama Islands) and Taiwan. Seen in pools formed
by seepage beside mountain forest roads; a mating behavior in which males
guard females for extended periods has been reported in academic research.

name: Common Micro Water Strider
description:
Broad-shouldered water strider family, genus Microvelia. *Microvelia douglasi*
Scott, 1874

About 1.5-2mm long, one of the smallest of the broad-shouldered water
striders. Found on Honshu, Shikoku, Kyushu, Tsushima, the Ryukyu Islands, and
the Daito Islands (Minami Daito-jima), and more widely abroad from the Korean
Peninsula through China, Southeast Asia, Taiwan, and Oceania. It prefers
flowing water such as small rice paddies and streams, and preys on small
insects that fall onto the water's surface. The family includes both wingless
forms that cannot fly and long-winged forms that can.

name: Lesser Diving Beetle
description:
Diving beetle family, genus Cybister. *Cybister tripunctatus orientalis*
Gschwendtner, 1931

Grows to about 24-29mm. Found on Honshu, Shikoku, Kyushu, the Ryukyu Islands,
and the Ogasawara Islands, and abroad in China, the Korean Peninsula, and
Taiwan. Elongate-oval and somewhat flattened, with a strongly glossy back
ranging from green to brownish black; a yellow rim along the edge of the
elytra is the key point for telling it apart from the tawny diving beetle. It
lives in ponds and marshes rich in aquatic plants, rice paddies and nearby
puddles, fallow fields, and slow-moving channels. Since the 1960s it has
declined sharply on Honshu and further south due to pesticide use and field
consolidation, and is listed as Vulnerable on the Ministry of the
Environment's Red List, but it is still relatively commonly seen in the
Ryukyu Islands. It closely resembles the tawny diving beetle in shape and
coloring, making the two difficult to tell apart from photographs alone.

name: Gracile Water Strider
description:
Water strider family, genus Gerris. *Gerris gracilicornis* (Horváth, 1879)

A large, reddish-brown water strider about 11-16mm long. Widely distributed across Japan, from Hokkaido through Honshu, Shikoku, Kyushu, and the Nansei Islands, it favors ponds, rivers, and marshes, especially cooler bodies of water. It overwinters as an adult on land and, after waking, flies off to find new water bodies, so it is often seen at small puddles in early spring.

name: Elongate Glossy Riffle Beetle
description:
Riffle beetle family, genus Zaitzevia. *Zaitzevia elongata* Nomura, 1962

A small aquatic beetle found in the Amami and Okinawa island groups. Eight
species of the genus Zaitzevia are known in Japan, with different species
distributed from Honshu to the Yaeyama Islands. Riffle beetles mainly live in
clean streams, but the detailed ecology of this species itself is still
largely unknown.

name: Nomura's Riffle Beetle
description:
Riffle beetle family, genus Stenelmis. *Stenelmis amami* Yoshitomi et Hayashi, 2021

A small aquatic beetle found in the Amami and Okinawa island groups. It was
originally treated as the sole species of its own genus, but a 2021 molecular
phylogenetic study (Kobayashi et al., 2021) placed it in the genus Stenelmis.
The genus name (Nomuraelmis) and the Japanese common name were coined in
1964 by Dr. Masataka Satô, and are thought to honor Dr. Nomura, who helped
pioneer riffle beetle research in Japan during that same era.
The detailed ecology of this species itself is still largely unknown.

name: Okinawa Striped Diving Beetle
description:
Diving beetle family, genus Hydaticus. *Hydaticus vittatus* (Fabricius, 1775)

Grows to about 11-14mm. A southern-type diving beetle found in the Ryukyu
Islands south of Yakushima, and abroad in Taiwan, China, and Southeast Asia.
Lives in still water such as ponds and rice paddies rich in aquatic plants.
In addition to habitat decline, many diving beetles, including this species,
have recently been found being sold for what appears to be the pet trade, so
in January 2023 it was designated, along with other diving beetles, a
Specified Second-Class Nationally Rare Wild Species. This designation only
regulates capture and transfer for the purpose of sale or distribution;
capturing it for observation is not restricted. It closely resembles a
related species of the same genus distributed west of Honshu, but the two
are easy to tell apart since their ranges do not overlap.

name: Ryukyu Broadchest Glossy Beetle
description:
Long-toed water beetle family (Dryopidae), genus Elmomorphus.
*Elmomorphus amamiensis* Nomura, 1959

A small aquatic beetle recorded on Amami Oshima and Okinoerabujima. It was
formerly treated as a Ryukyu-island subspecies of a mainland species, but in
2014 a study using COI gene sequencing and morphological comparison found a
major genetic divergence at the species level between the two, and it was
elevated to full species status. It is now generally accepted as a distinct
species. The Dryopidae are a family closely related to the riffle beetles
(Elmidae) and likewise live in clean streams. The detailed ecology of this
species itself is still largely unknown.

name: Sato's Riffle Beetle
description:
Riffle beetle family, genus Sinonychus. *Sinonychus satoi* Yoshitomi & Nakajima, 2007

A small aquatic beetle found in the Amami and Okinawa island groups (no record
from Okinawa Island itself), described in 2007. Only two species of the genus
Sinonychus are known in Japan; the other is found in Kyushu. The detailed
ecology of this species itself is still largely unknown.

name: Tsutsui's Stream Water Strider
description:
Broad-shouldered water strider family, genus Pseudovelia (stream water
striders). *Pseudovelia tsutsuii* Esaki & Miyamoto, 1955

Found in the Ryukyu Islands (from Takarajima to Okinawa Island). Several
species of the genus Pseudovelia are known in Japan, a group that lives along
the banks of rivers and ponds. Sufficient information on the detailed ecology
of this species itself has not yet been confirmed.

name: Ueno's Glossy Riffle Beetle
description:
Riffle beetle family, genus Urumaelmis. *Urumaelmis uenoi uenoi* (Nomura, 1961)

A small aquatic beetle found from Yakushima through the Amami
island group to the Okinawa island group (nominate subspecies). The genus Urumaelmis also includes a
second species newly described from Kyushu in 2020, bringing the number of
known species in Japan to two. The population on Kuchinoshima in the Tokara
Islands is distinguished as a separate subspecies (*U. u. tokarana*). The detailed ecology of
this species itself is still largely unknown.

name: Pale Striped Diving Beetle
description:
Diving beetle family, genus Hydaticus (striped diving beetles).
*Hydaticus rhantoides* Sharp, 1882

A small diving beetle about 10-11mm long. The elytra are overall yellowish
brown with no conspicuous striping. Found on Honshu (west of the Kanto
region), Shikoku, Kyushu, Tsushima, the Ryukyu Islands, and the Daito Islands,
and abroad in China, Taiwan, and Southeast Asia. Lives in open still water
such as rice paddies and ponds. Among the diving beetles of the Ryukyu
Islands, it is considered, along with the tawny diving beetle and the lesser
diving beetle, to be relatively holding its own in numbers.

name: Amami Hairy Dung Beetle
description:
Scarabaeidae, subfamily Aphodiinae, Amami Hairy Dung Beetle *Gilletianus atsushii* (Ochi, 1986)

A rare dung beetle found on Amami Oshima, with very few collection records. It was described in 1986 by Teruo Ochi as *Aphodius (Trichaphodius) atsushii*, but later taxonomic revisions placed it in the genus Gilletianus. It is thought to live off the droppings of the Amami rabbit, but much about its ecology remains unknown, and records of it are limited.

name: Amami Small Rhinoceros Beetle
description:
Scarabaeidae, subfamily Dynastinae, Amami Small Rhinoceros Beetle *Eophileurus chinensis irregularis* Prell, 1913

A subspecies of the small rhinoceros beetle *Eophileurus chinensis*, found on Amami Oshima, Tokunoshima, Yoro, and Uke. Males reach about 20–25mm and females about 15–20mm. It lives in forests from lowlands to mountains, and is nocturnal, often seen walking on the forest floor or along forest roads; from early summer to late autumn it also comes to sap and lights. Adults can be seen nearly year-round, though it is not a particularly abundant species.

name: Amami Mottled Dung Beetle
description:
Scarabaeidae, subfamily Aphodiinae, Amami Mottled Dung Beetle *Chilothorax ohishii* (Masumoto, 1975)

An endemic species found only on Amami Oshima and Tokunoshima. It was described in 1975 by Toshiya Masumoto as *Aphodius ohishii*, but is now placed in the genus Chilothorax. It feeds mainly on the droppings of the Amami rabbit, and is commonly seen from autumn through spring, while rarely appearing in summer.

name: Amami Green Jewel Beetle
description:
Buprestidae, Amami Green Jewel Beetle *Chalcophora japonica oshimana* Schönfeldt, 1890

Body length 24–40mm. A subspecies, found in the Amami and Okinawa island groups, of the jewel beetle *Chalcophora japonica*, which is widely distributed from Hokkaido to Okinawa. It favors dead or weakened pine trees, and the larvae feed and grow inside the wood. Adults are seen from early summer into summer.

name: Bates's Flat Longhorn Beetle
description:
Cerambycidae, Bates's Flat Longhorn Beetle *Eurypoda batesi* Gahan, 1894

Body length 26–34mm. Widely distributed from Honshu (south of the Kanto and Chubu regions) through Shikoku, Kyushu, and the Nansei Islands north of Okinawa Island (including Amami Oshima and Tokunoshima), and also found outside Japan on the Korean Peninsula and in southwestern China. It gathers on camphor, chinquapin, and machilus trees, is nocturnal, and also comes to lights. Commonly seen from around June to August.

name: Ferrié's Red Longhorn Beetle
description:
Cerambycidae, Ferrié's Red Longhorn Beetle *Rosalia (Eurybatus) ferriei* Vuillet, 1911

An endemic species found only on Amami Oshima. It has a beautiful red body marked with black patterns, and appears on standing dead trees deep in the forest around July. It is named after Father Ferrié, who collected the species on Amami Oshima. It is designated a Rare Wild Species under Kagoshima Prefecture's ordinance for the protection of rare wildlife, and its capture or collection is prohibited.

name: Amami Round Dung Beetle
description:
Scarabaeidae, subfamily Coprinae, Amami Round Dung Beetle *Copris brachypterus* Nomura, 1964

Body length 13–20mm. An endemic species found only on Amami Oshima and Tokunoshima (a different subspecies occurs on Tokunoshima); its hind wings are reduced, so it cannot fly. At night it walks through mountain forests searching for the droppings of the Amami rabbit, and has the habit of digging a hole beneath a dung ball and dragging it in backwards with its front legs. Because its range is extremely limited, it has poor mobility, and past collection pressure has significantly reduced its numbers, it is listed as Vulnerable (VU) on the Ministry of the Environment's Red List.

name: Green Narrow Jewel Beetle
description:
Buprestidae, Green Narrow Jewel Beetle *Coraebus hastanus oberthueri*

A small jewel beetle about 11mm long, found from Amami Oshima southward. Members of the genus Coraebus are known to be most active during the strong sunlight of summer, and this species too is seen from around June to September.

name: Large Green Leaf Beetle
description:
Chrysomelidae, Large Green Leaf Beetle *Platycorynus japonicus*

Body length about 10mm. A small leaf beetle with a metallic green sheen, found in the Nansei Islands (from Amami Oshima southward). It feeds on plants of the star jasmine group, and is seen from around April to October.

name: Oshima Earth-boring Dung Beetle
description:
Geotrupidae, Oshima Earth-boring Dung Beetle *Phelotrupes oshimanus* Fairmaire, 1895

Reaching 20mm in length, this is the largest species of Geotrupidae found in Japan. An endemic species found only on Amami Oshima and Tokunoshima, it is active from autumn into winter and gathers at the droppings of the Amami rabbit and wild boar. It has the distinctive habit of cradling dung with its front legs and dragging it backwards into its own burrow. It is listed as Near Threatened on the Kagoshima Prefecture Red List.

name: Oshima Tiger Flower Chafer
description:
Scarabaeidae, Oshima Tiger Flower Chafer *Paratrichius duplicatus duplicatus* Lewis, 1895

Body length 11.8–15.6mm. The nominate subspecies (P. d. duplicatus), found on Amami Oshima and Tokunoshima; a different subspecies, the Okinawa Tiger Flower Chafer (P. d. okinawanus), occurs in the Okinawa island group. Compared with related tiger flower chafers, its wing covers are tinged darker, giving it a distinctive sheen. It appears from April to May.

name: Azure Narrow Jewel Beetle
description:
Buprestidae, Azure Narrow Jewel Beetle *Coraebus niponicus* Lewis, 1894

A small jewel beetle with an azure sheen, recorded on Amami Oshima. Members of the genus Coraebus are known to be most active during the strong sunlight of summer, and this species too is seen from around June to September.

name: Coconut Rhinoceros Beetle
description:
Scarabaeidae, subfamily Dynastinae, Coconut Rhinoceros Beetle *Oryctes rhinoceros* (Linnaeus, 1758)

An invasive species native to the Indochina Peninsula region. The first record in Japan is believed to be its introduction to Ishigaki Island in imported materials from Taiwan in the early 20th century; it subsequently spread northward, and was confirmed on Amami Oshima and Tokunoshima in 1991. It is now established and breeding naturally across nearly the entire Nansei Islands. It is known as an agricultural pest that bores into the stems and cores of palms, pineapple, and sugarcane, and there is concern about competition with native rhinoceros beetle species.

name: Tokara Pill Scarab
description:
Ceratocanthidae, subfamily Ceratocanthinae, Tokara Pill Scarab *Madrasostes kazumai* Ochi, Johki et Nakata, 1990

A small beetle about 5.0–5.8mm long, found in the Tokara Islands (the type locality is Nakanoshima) and on Amami Oshima. It is distinguished by range from the closely related Sakishima Pill Scarab (*M. kazumai hisamatsui* Ochi, 1990), found in the Yaeyama Islands. It is considered a myrmecophilous species — found in environments close to ant nests, such as inside rotten wood or in the leaf litter layer around it — and the original description's paper title itself uses the word "myrmecophilous." When disturbed, it withdraws its antennae and legs into its body and rolls up into a perfect ball, like a pill bug, to protect itself.

name: Chinese Sparrowhawk
description:
Hawk family (Accipitridae), genus Tachyspiza. *Tachyspiza soloensis* (until a
2024 taxonomic revision, classified as *Accipiter soloensis*)

A small hawk about 30 cm long that does not breed in Japan, passing through
only in spring and autumn as a migrant. The upperparts are dark bluish-gray
and the underparts pale orange-brown, with reddish-brown eyes in males and
yellow eyes in females. It breeds from northeastern China through the Korean
Peninsula and winters in Southeast Asia. Spring passage also occurs, but
Amami Oshima sees its largest numbers in autumn, when the passage peaks from
mid-September through October as cicadas and dragonflies that serve as prey
become abundant; flocks can sometimes be seen circling upward together on
rising air currents in what is called a "hawk pillar." It preys widely on
small animals such as frogs, insects, and lizards. It is listed as Least
Concern on the IUCN Red List and is not subject to designation under Japan's
Ministry of the Environment Red List or Act on Conservation of Endangered
Species.

name: Ryukyu Robin
description:
Old World flycatcher family (Muscicapidae), genus Larvivora.
*Larvivora komadori*

About 14 cm long, weighing about 18 g. A species endemic to Japan that
breeds from the Danjo Islands through the Tokara Islands, Amami Oshima and
its surrounding islets, to Tokunoshima; designated a Natural Monument in
1970. It is a year-round resident on Amami Oshima, but males sing especially
often to proclaim territory during the breeding season from March to June,
so following the song early in the morning is the best way to find one at
that time of year. Males have a vivid orange-red head, back, and tail, and
the black patches on the breast and flanks look like a "beard," which gives
the species its Japanese name. Females are overall plainer in color. It
forages for insects on the forest floor of evergreen broadleaf forest. A
different species lives in northern Okinawa Island, but the two ranges do
not overlap.

name: Amami Woodcock
description:
Sandpiper family (Scolopacidae), genus Scolopax. *Scolopax mira*

About 35-36 cm long. A species endemic to Japan found only in the Amami and
Okinawa island groups, with breeding confirmed on Amami Oshima, Kakeromajima,
Uke-jima, Yoro-jima, and Tokunoshima. It resembles the closely related
Eurasian woodcock but has longer legs, an overall blacker tone, and a
stockier build than other sandpipers. It prefers the dim forest floor of
evergreen broadleaf forest, is most active from dusk to dawn, and forages on
the ground for earthworms and insects. It becomes especially active in the
dim light of early morning and evening, and on moonlit nights. The breeding
season runs from around February to May, and at dusk males perform a
courtship and territorial "roding" display flight, making this the easiest
time of year to spot one. It nests on the ground within forests and lays
2-4 eggs from around March through May. Designated a Nationally Rare Wild
Species in 1993. Following the eradication of the small Indian mongoose and
forest recovery as logging has declined, its population has been gradually
recovering, and in March 2026 the Ministry of the Environment's 5th Red List
downgraded its status from Vulnerable (VU) to Near Threatened (NT). Predation
by feral cats remains an ongoing concern.

name: Blue Rock Thrush
description:
Old World flycatcher family (Muscicapidae), genus Monticola. *Monticola
solitarius*

About 23 cm long. Males and females look very different: males are blue from
the head to the back with reddish-brown underparts, while females are
grayish-brown with dark scaly barring. A year-round resident on Amami
Oshima, it traditionally favors rocky coastlines and harbors — as its
Japanese name ("rocky shore thrush") suggests — but in recent years it has
been spreading inland and into towns across Japan, and on Amami it is
increasingly seen around houses, on rooftops, power lines, and in parking
lots. A strongly predatory bird, it feeds on crustaceans, insects, lizards,
and even small rodents, and sings a high, clear, elaborate song. It is
solitary and holds a year-round territory; breeding is thought to begin
around March.

name: Common Kingfisher
description:
Kingfisher family (Alcedinidae), genus Alcedo. *Alcedo atthis bengalensis*

About 17 cm long and weighing 19-40 g, a small kingfisher. The head and
back have a glossy blue-green sheen and the underparts are a vivid orange,
earning it the nickname "jewel of the water's edge." On Amami Oshima it is
a year-round resident found along rivers, irrigation channels beside rice
paddies, and ponds of many kinds. It watches the water from a perch on an
overhanging branch or post, then plunges in to catch small fish or shrimp
as soon as it spots one. Strongly territorial, it lives alone or in pairs
and digs a tunnel nest into a riverbank or eroded slope. The breeding
season runs from around March to August, and pairs may raise more than one
brood; courtship includes the male passing a small fish to the female,
known as courtship feeding, and the birds are especially active and easy
to watch during this period. Unlike most of the birds on this site, it can
be watched by daylight at the water's edge rather than in the night
forest.

name: Black-faced Spoonbill
description:
Ibis family (Threskiornithidae), genus Platalea. *Platalea minor*

A large waterbird about 70-80 cm long. The whole body is white, and, as its
name suggests, it has a distinctive black, spoon-shaped bill and black skin
around the eyes. During the breeding season it grows a crest and its breast
takes on a yellowish tinge. It can be told apart from the closely related
Eurasian Spoonbill by the black facial skin, which extends broadly to the
base of the bill. It breeds on islands off the west coast of the Korean
Peninsula and the coast of northeastern China, and winters in Taiwan, Hong
Kong, southern China, Japan, and elsewhere. The world population fell to
around 300 birds in the early 1990s, but conservation efforts have driven a
recovery, and the 2025 international census counted more than 7,000. In
Japan, numbers arriving are on the rise, mainly in Kyushu, and on Amami
Oshima it too is observed on tidal flats and similar sites from winter
through spring. It was designated a Nationally Rare Wild Species under the
Act on Conservation of Endangered Species in 2020, prohibiting capture and
transfer (the Natural Monument designation applies not to the species
itself but to certain habitat sites within Kagoshima Prefecture). Around
2025 the IUCN Red List downgraded its status from Endangered (EN) to
Vulnerable (VU).

name: Amami Thrush
description:
Old World flycatcher family (Muscicapidae), genus Zoothera.
*Zoothera dauma major*

About 30 cm long. A resident bird found only on Amami Oshima, with a
yellowish-brown ground color marked with black, tiger-like blotches.
Designated a national Natural Monument and a Nationally Rare Wild Species.
It prefers the dim forest floor of mature broadleaf forest and feeds on
earthworms and the like. During the breeding season from February to early
April, it sings a clear, beautiful "kyoroon, tsi-i" call in the dim light
before dawn and at dusk. It once declined so sharply due to logging and the
impact of invasive species that it was called a "phantom bird," but as the
forest has recovered, its population has been on a recovering trend in
recent years, and in March 2026 the Ministry of the Environment's 5th Red
List downgraded its status from Vulnerable (VU) to Near Threatened (NT).

name: Owston's Woodpecker
description:
Woodpecker family (Picidae), genus Dendrocopos.
*Dendrocopos leucotos owstoni*

About 28 cm long, a medium-sized woodpecker. An endemic subspecies found
only on Amami Oshima; the upper body is almost entirely black with white
spots, and the underside is a stronger brown than in other subspecies. The
crown is red in males and black in females, making the sexes easy to tell
apart. It lives mainly in mature laurel forest and excavates nest holes in
the trunks of large broadleaf trees. It feeds mainly on longhorn beetle
larvae hidden in rotten wood. Territorial proclamations and courtship
displays begin around winter, and from February through May its
"drumming" — rapid pecking at a trunk with its bill — and calls are easiest
to hear. In recent years its range has expanded across the whole of Amami
Oshima, partly due to the effects of pine wilt disease. Since the only
other woodpecker on Amami Oshima is the Amami pygmy woodpecker, the two can
be told apart by size alone. Designated a national Natural Monument in 1971
and a Nationally Rare Wild Species in 1993; capture and transfer are
prohibited.

name: Lidth's Jay
description:
Crow family (Corvidae), genus Garrulus. *Garrulus lidthi*

About 38 cm long. A species endemic to Japan found only on Amami Oshima,
Kakeromajima, and Uke-jima, beautiful with its azure-blue body, reddish-brown
wings, and white bill and wingtips. Designated a Natural Monument in 1921.
It prefers evergreen broadleaf forest and is omnivorous, feeding on
chinquapin and oak acorns. Nest-building begins around December, and during
the breeding season from around February through May it lays 3-7 eggs in a
tree hollow or similar site; late February through early April, when
parent birds move about actively near the nest, is an especially good time
to spot one. Its numbers once declined due to
predation by feral cats and the introduced small Indian mongoose, but
conservation efforts have paid off — including the 2024 declaration of
mongoose eradication — and its population has been recovering in recent
years. It flies about actively during the day, but at night it can be
observed resting on power lines or branch tips along forest roads.

name: Ryukyu Ruddy Kingfisher
description:
Kingfisher family (Alcedinidae), genus Halcyon. *Halcyon coromanda bangsi*

About 27 cm long, its whole body a glossy reddish-brown, with a pale-blue
patch on the rump that stands out clearly in flight. Locally on Amami
Oshima it is also known as "Kukkaru," and is loved for its far-carrying
"kyororororo" call. It is a summer migrant that arrives from its
Southeast Asian wintering grounds around the end of April, near Japan's
Golden Week holidays, and heads south again by around September. Despite
belonging to the kingfisher family, it eats relatively little fish,
preying widely on crabs, frogs, lizards, and insects of the forest. During
the breeding season from June to July it lays around five eggs in a tree
hollow or an old woodpecker nest, and the chicks fledge around July. Parent
birds become especially nervous during this period; approaching the nest
tree, making noise, or using flash photography can cause them to abandon
the nest or force the chicks to fledge early, so it is best to watch
quietly from a distance and for only a short time.

name: Ryukyu Whistling Green-Pigeon
description:
Pigeon family (Columbidae), genus Treron. *Treron permagnus*

About 35 cm long, somewhat larger than the White-bellied Green-Pigeon, and
a year-round resident. Its whole body is a vivid green. The Japanese name,
meaning "red-headed green-pigeon," comes from the reddish head of its
close relative the Taiwan Whistling Green-Pigeon (Treron formosae), but
this species, found on Amami Oshima and elsewhere, is green even on the
head. It lives in laurel forest from lowlands to mountains and feeds in
the trees on fruit and seeds, including that of Ficus erecta. It gives a
distinctive shakuhachi-like call, "oo-ao, pe, hepo." It breeds around May,
laying two eggs. Due to habitat fragmentation and decline, it is listed as
Near Threatened on the IUCN Red List.

name: Ryukyu Scops Owl
description:
Owl family (Strigidae), genus Otus. *Otus elegans elegans*

About 22 cm long, one of the smallest owls found in Japan. The whole body
is brown with fine, moth-eaten-looking mottling. It is a year-round
resident found from Amami Oshima southward through the Ryukyu Islands,
occurring not only in mature forest but also in woodland near houses.
Nocturnal, after sunset it repeats a low "koho, koho" call, and the female
sometimes answers with a "nya." It preys on insects, spiders, and geckos.
It nests in tree hollows, old woodpecker holes, or among the fronds of
bird's-nest fern, and lays 4-5 eggs during the breeding season from April
to around July. Only the female incubates, but both parents share the
work of feeding the chicks, and most fledge around July. Around the time
of fledging, chicks are still unsteady in flight and may be found perched
on branches close to the ground; rather than picking them up or shining
a light on them for long periods, it is best to quietly leave the area.
The call itself can be heard year-round, not only during the breeding
season.

name: Ryukyu Paradise Flycatcher
description:
Monarch flycatcher family (Monarchidae), genus Terpsiphone.
*Terpsiphone atrocaudata illex*

Males measure about 45 cm including the tail streamers, females about 18
cm. The whole body has a black-purple sheen, and the eye-ring and bill are
a vivid cobalt blue. Males have tail feathers nearly three times the
length of the body, giving them a striking silhouette in flight. On Amami
Oshima it arrives as a summer migrant around April and, in the dim
interior of the forest, flits from branch to branch catching flying
insects such as small flies, wasps, and butterflies in mid-air. Its call
is said to sound like "tsuki-hi-hoshi, hoi-hoi-hoi" ("moon, sun, stars,
hoi-hoi-hoi"), which is why it is named the "three-light bird" after these
three lights. From May to July it builds a cup-shaped nest of moss in the
fork of a tree and shares incubation and chick-rearing duties. While
unfledged chicks are in the nest, lingering close by or shaking the
branch can cause the parents to abandon it, so it is best to watch briefly
through binoculars from a distance. It heads back to its Southeast Asian
wintering grounds around September.

name: Grey-faced Buzzard
description:
Hawk family (Accipitridae), genus Butastur. *Butastur indicus*

Males are about 47 cm long and females about 51 cm, with a wingspan of
105-115 cm; a medium-sized hawk. The head is grayish-brown, the upperparts
and breast are brown, and the throat is white with a black central streak.
It preys mainly on small animals such as snakes, lizards, and frogs, as
well as insects like cicadas and grasshoppers. It breeds in Kyushu and
northward through Honshu and Shikoku, and once breeding is finished, birds
migrate south from early September through the Nansei Islands toward
Southeast Asia. Amami Oshima is known as Japan's largest wintering ground
for the species, with the passage peaking around mid-October, when large
numbers of birds can be seen circling and rising together in what is
called a "hawk pillar." Many birds do not complete the journey south and
instead winter on the island; an estimated 2,000 or so stay from November
through around March. It is listed as Vulnerable on the Ministry of the
Environment's Red List and on Appendix II of CITES. Around the forests
used as roosts, avoid loud noises, sudden movements, and flash photography
that could startle the birds into unnecessary flight, and observe quietly
from a distance.

name: Black-winged Stilt
description:
Stilt family (Recurvirostridae), genus Himantopus. *Himantopus himantopus*

About 37-40 cm long, a shorebird with extremely long, reddish legs and a
thin black bill. The body is white with black wings and back; males show
more black extending to the back of the head, while females are paler. It
feeds on aquatic insects, crustaceans, shellfish, and small fish. In Japan
it was first confirmed breeding at reclaimed land in Aichi Prefecture in
1975 and has since become locally established in parts of Honshu, but in
the Nansei Islands it occurs mainly as a passage migrant and winter
visitor. Within Kagoshima Prefecture it has been recorded on Amami Oshima,
Tokunoshima, and Nakanoshima in the Tokara Islands, and breeding was
confirmed on nearby Okinoerabujima in 2009, though there are few records of
breeding on Amami Oshima itself, or of exactly when it arrives there. It
favors shallow water such as tidal flats, rice paddies, and fallow fields.
It was previously classified as Vulnerable (VU) on the Ministry of the
Environment Red List but is now listed as Data Deficient (DD).

name: Northern Lapwing
description:
Plover family (Charadriidae), genus Vanellus. *Vanellus vanellus*

About 32 cm long, with a long crest on the head, a back with a glossy
greenish-black sheen, and a white belly. Its elegant appearance has earned
it the nickname "winter lady." It breeds across Eurasia and visits Japan
as a winter migrant. On Amami Oshima it begins to appear in open farmland
such as rice paddies and fields from around late October, staying through
the winter until around late March or April of the following year. It
moves in flocks, foraging in the soil for earthworms and insects. Unlike
the creatures of the night forest that this site mainly features, it is a
messenger of winter that is easy to observe by day in open farmland.

name: Long-eared Owl
description:
Owl family (Strigidae), genus Asio. *Asio otus*

About 35-40 cm long, an owl notable for the long, ear-like tufts of
feathers on its head. The upperparts are grayish to pale brown with
streaking, and the eyes are orange. It breeds as a summer visitor in
Hokkaido and northern Honshu, but from central Honshu southward it occurs
mainly as a winter visitor. The only owls resident year-round on Amami
Oshima are the Ryukyu Scops Owl and the Ryukyu Brown Hawk-Owl; aside from
these, a small number of Long-eared Owls arrive as winter visitors each
year, typically appearing from around November. Outside the breeding
season it is known to form communal roosts, gathering in groups in
evergreen trees or bamboo thickets. It preys mainly on small mammals such
as rodents, as well as insects and small birds. Few individuals reach Amami
Oshima, and because they are quite wary, they can be difficult to observe.

name: Barbour's Skink
description:
Skink family (Scincidae), genus Plestiodon. *Plestiodon barbouri*

Total length 15.5-20 cm (snout-vent length 5.2-7.3 cm). A species endemic to
Japan, distributed on Amami Oshima, Kakeromajima, Uke-jima, Yoro-jima,
Tokunoshima, and the Okinawa Islands. Juveniles are blackish brown with five
bright longitudinal stripes, and a vivid blue tail that makes up more than
two-thirds of the total tail length. As they grow, the blue fades; males
become overall dark brown to brown, while many females retain coloring
closer to that of juveniles. It prefers the forest floor and edges of
natural evergreen broadleaf forest or well-recovered secondary forest,
basking in the sun to regulate its body temperature while feeding on
spiders and land snails. It becomes sluggish in winter but does not
hibernate. Its numbers have declined due to drying of habitat from logging
and undergrowth clearance, and predation by feral cats and the introduced
small Indian mongoose. It is listed as Vulnerable on the Ministry of the
Environment's Red List, and in 2019 was also designated a Kagoshima
Prefecture Rare Wildlife Species, making unauthorized capture or collection
subject to penalties.

name: Amami Rabbit
description:
Rabbit family (Leporidae), genus Pentalagus. *Pentalagus furnessi*

Grows to about 41-51 cm and weighs 1.3-2.7 kg. A species endemic to Japan,
found only on Amami Oshima and Tokunoshima, and often called a "living
fossil" for retaining strongly primitive features. Designated a Natural
Monument in 1921 and a Special Natural Monument in 1963. Nocturnal, it bases
its activity around burrows dug in rock crevices or tree hollows, feeding on
chinquapin nuts and young shoots. Breeding occurs mainly in spring and
autumn, with one young born per litter. Its numbers once declined due to
predation by feral cats and the introduced small Indian mongoose, but as
mongoose eradication efforts have progressed, the population has been
recovering in recent years. It is the emblematic animal of night tours, and
it is not uncommon to encounter one hopping along a forest road.

name: Ryukyu Long-haired Rat
description:
Rat family (Muridae), genus Diplothrix. *Diplothrix legata*

Body length 22-33 cm, tail length 25-35 cm. Japan's largest rat, found only
on Amami Oshima, Tokunoshima, and the northern part of Okinawa Island, with
long bristle-like hairs of 5-6 cm mixed into its coat. Designated a Natural
Monument in 1972 and a Nationally Rare Wild Species in 2016. Nocturnal and
strongly arboreal, it rests during the day in tree-hollow nests lined with
dead leaves. Omnivorous, feeding on chinquapin nuts and insects among other
things. Breeds from autumn into early winter, giving birth to 2-5 young per
litter. It is not very wary, and since it does not flee much even when a
flashlight is shone on it, it can sometimes be observed at leisure along
forest roads.

name: Watase's Shrew
description:
Shrew family (Soricidae), genus Crocidura. *Crocidura watasei*

One of the world's smallest mammals, about 5.5 cm long and weighing just 5-8
g. A species endemic to Japan, found only in the Amami island group (Amami
Oshima, Kakeromajima, Tokunoshima, and others) and the Okinawa Islands. It
prefers open environments such as grassland and farmland, and feeds on small
insects and spiders. Nocturnal, it can sometimes be seen darting quickly
through grassy patches beside forest roads. It differs in habitat from a
forest-dwelling relative of the same genus, and the two are sometimes
confused. It carries no legal capture restriction like a Natural Monument
designation, but it is listed as Near Threatened by the Ministry of the
Environment.

name: Amami Flat Pygmy Grasshopper
description:
Pygmy grasshopper family, Amami Flat Pygmy Grasshopper *Austrohancockia amamiensis* Yamasaki, 1994

A species endemic to Japan, found on Amami Oshima and Tokunoshima. Body length is about 10mm in males and about 14.5mm in females. Its flattened, broadly spread pronotum is distinctive, and it lives on the leaf-littered forest floor, camouflaged to match its surroundings. It moves quickly and leaps away when startled.

name: Common Bluebottle
description:
Swallowtail family, Common Bluebottle *Graphium sarpedon nipponum* Fruhstorfer, 1903

A fast-flying, striking swallowtail with a band of blue-green running across both wings on an otherwise black background. It feeds on camphor-family trees such as camphor and machilus, and is seen island-wide on Amami Oshima. With several generations a year, it remains on the wing for a long stretch of the warmer months.

name: Amami Longwing Dragonfly
description:
Skimmer family, Amami Longwing Dragonfly *Rhyothemis severini* Ris, 1913

A rare dragonfly confirmed in Japan only on Amami Oshima. Its body is black with a deep green sheen, and its clear wings carry indigo markings. It favors ponds thick with emergent vegetation, where males patrol low over the water waiting for females. Because its habitat and population are extremely limited, it is designated a Nationally Rare Species of Wild Fauna and Flora under Japan's Act on Conservation of Endangered Species, and capture is prohibited.

name: Common Map Butterfly
description:
Brush-footed butterfly family, Common Map Butterfly *Cyrestis thyodamas* Boisduval, 1836

A butterfly with truly distinctive wings — a white ground crossed by a dark brown, tortoiseshell-like pattern. Found from the Kii Peninsula westward through the Nansei Islands, including Amami Oshima. Larvae feed on fig-family plants such as Ficus erecta and banyan. It overwinters as an adult and produces repeated generations from spring into late autumn during the warmer months.

name: Rotten Wood Cricket
description:
Bush cricket family (Eneopteridae) Rotten Wood Cricket *Duolandrevus ivani*

A somewhat large cricket-like insect, 31–35mm long. Widely distributed across the Nansei Islands, including Amami Oshima and Tokunoshima, it lives hidden beneath the bark of rotting wood, as its Japanese name suggests. At night it calls with a distinctive "gwiii, gwiii." In warm regions, adults can be seen year-round regardless of season.

name: Spotted Bush Cricket
description:
Bush cricket family (Eneopteridae) Spotted Bush Cricket *Cardiodactylus guttulus*

Although its Japanese name means "cricket," it is taxonomically a bush cricket. It lives in the forests of the Nansei Islands south of the Tokara Islands, and in the Amami Islands adults appear from around late August. It often gathers on tree trunks day and night, calling with a sharp "chit, chit" sound. It is abundant and serves as an important food source for reptiles and birds.

name: Round-spot Raspy Cricket
description:
Raspy cricket family (Gryllacrididae) Round-spot Raspy Cricket *Prosopogryllacris okadai* Ichikawa, 2001

An arboreal raspy cricket found on Takara Island, Amami Oshima, and Kakeroma Island. Its antennae are far longer than its body. By day it hides in a nest of leaves bound together with its own silk, emerging at night to be active. Strongly carnivorous, it preys on other insects. It is very wary and difficult to spot.

name: Okinawa Variegated Flutterer
description:
Skimmer family, Okinawa Variegated Flutterer *Rhyothemis variegata imperatrix* Selys, 1887

A subspecies of the Variegated Flutterer found across the Nansei Islands, seen widely from Amami Oshima through Okinawa, Miyako, and the Yaeyama Islands. About 40mm long, with dark brown wing markings that vary considerably in size and shape between individuals. Fluttering around ponds and rice paddies, it flies with a butterfly-like, flitting motion.

name: Great Ring-spot Moth
description:
Owlet moth family (Erebidae in recent classification) Great Ring-spot Moth *Erebus ephesperis* (Hübner, [1823])

The largest of the tomoe moths, with a wingspan reaching 90–100mm. Its brown wings have a wavy, undulating edge and a ring-shaped white marking on the forewing — the source of its Japanese name, meaning "great comma." The larvae feed on Smilax (catbrier) plants, and the adults also come to lights. On Amami Oshima, it has also been documented academically as a pollinator of Hoya (wax vine) flowers.

name: Blue Tiger
description:
Brush-footed butterfly family, Blue Tiger *Ideopsis similis* (Linnaeus, 1758)

A milkweed butterfly with pale blue markings, gliding gracefully and unhurriedly through the air. Found from Amami Oshima southward, its larvae feed on Marsdenia tinctoria. On winter days when the temperature drops below 15°C, hundreds can be seen clustering together to overwinter in the forests of the island's valleys — a well-known winter scene on Amami Oshima.

name: Giant Katydid
description:
Katydid family (Tettigoniidae) Giant Katydid *Mecopoda elongata* (Linnaeus, 1758)

A katydid found in warm regions from the Izu Peninsula southward, including Amami Oshima and the rest of the Nansei Islands. It begins calling in late summer, and as autumn deepens it sings loudly with a rattling "gyururururu." Its early calls are spaced apart — "gyuu, gyuu" — before gradually becoming one continuous, unbroken sound.

name: Akamata Snake
description:
Colubrid snake family, genus Dinodon. *Dinodon semicarinatum*

Grows up to about 200 cm. Most easily observed from May through November. The body is
yellowish brown with red-and-black oval crossbands. It has no venom but is aggressive,
hissing and striking if you enter its territory. It feeds on mammals, birds, reptiles,
amphibians, and fish, and even eats sea turtle eggs; it sometimes preys on its natural
enemy, the Habu pit viper. Nocturnal, it can be seen along forest roads and around water,
all the way to the coast. Smaller individuals show stronger red coloring and are very
beautiful, but even a small one gives a painful bite, so take care.

name: Amami Odd-scaled Snake
description:
Takachiho snake family, Takachiho tribe. *Achalinus werneri*

Grows up to about 55 cm. The back is blackish brown or dark brown with a black stripe
running along the midline; the belly is yellow. On Amami it is a legendary snake that you
only encounter under just the right conditions. It sometimes comes to the surface on days
of heavy rain. Nocturnal and subterranean, it lives in forests, grassy areas near water,
and farmland. It feeds on earthworms. It is scarcer and harder to find here than the
Amami odd-scaled snakes on other islands. It is very slender and small, so you may not
notice it even if you drive right past.

name: Pryer's Keelback
description:
Colubrid snake family, genus Hebius. *Hebius pryeri*

Grows up to about 110 cm. Most easily observed from May through November. Slender-bodied,
with a black or blackish-brown color and yellow or brown banding along the body. It
prefers watery habitats and is often found around rice paddies and other spots with
plenty of small frogs. It is venomous, but its fangs for injecting venom are small, and a
bite alone is said not to introduce much venom into the body — even so, the venom itself
is quite potent, so caution is needed. It feeds on frogs, fish, geckos, and small lizards.
It moves quickly, but will threaten you if it senses danger.

name: Habu Pit Viper
description:
Pit viper family, genus Protobothrops. *Protobothrops flavoviridis*

Grows up to about 226 cm, one of the largest snakes on the island. Most active and easiest to
observe from May through November (it may also move on warm days even in winter). Nocturnal,
resting in burrows and crevices during the day. Found from lowland forests to mountain forests,
grasslands, wetlands, farmland, and even trees, and it sometimes enters areas near houses while
hunting rats. Feeds mainly on rats, as well as reptiles, frogs, mammals, and birds. Natural
enemies include the Akamata snake and human hunters. Venomous and highly aggressive. Always
keep a distance of at least 2-3 meters when observing or photographing. If approached, it does
not flee — it immediately takes a striking posture and can lunge roughly two-thirds of its own
body length. A bite deep in the mountains, where there is no phone signal, can become a serious
emergency. Its pattern blends into the forest floor and is very hard to spot; it may be hiding
nearby even when you can't see it. You cannot be too careful.

name: Okinawa Pit Viper
description:
Pit viper family, genus Ovophis. *Ovophis okinavensis*

Grows up to about 80 cm. Cold-tolerant, and on Amami Oshima it can be observed
year-round. Once the rainy season ends and the weather turns hot, it is often seen at
higher elevations. It feeds on small to medium-sized frogs, small mammals, and birds. It
is commonly observed in places with plenty of frogs, such as rice paddies and
slow-flowing streams. A coiled individual barely moves, but it will threaten you if you
enter its territory. It is a venomous snake, so if bitten, go to a hospital immediately.
Be careful not to step on it.

name: Ryukyu Coral Snake
description:
Cobra family, genus Sinomicrurus (also known as the Ryukyu coral snake). *Sinomicrurus
japonicus*

Grows up to about 50 cm. Most easily observed around May and around September. The back
is reddish-brown or orange with five dark brown longitudinal stripes. It is designated a
"Specified Dangerous Animal," a legal category for species considered capable of harming
people. Its venom is neurotoxic and stronger than the Habu's, but its head is small and
its temperament is docile. If picked up, it will jab you with its tail, which is as hard
as bone. It is nocturnal and scarce, so sightings are rare. It is popular enough that some
people visit Amami Oshima specifically hoping to see one.

name: Ryukyu Green Snake
description:
Colubrid snake family, genus Cycophuops. *Cycophuops semicarinatus*

Grows up to about 100 cm. Most easily observed from May through November. Mainly
diurnal, though many individuals are also active at night. It has a small head and feeds
mainly on earthworms, as well as frogs. It is the most numerous snake on Amami Oshima and
can be seen in forests during the day and along forest roads at night. Larger individuals
will sometimes threaten you, but they flee very quickly, sliding down slopes to escape.

name: Amami Flat Stag Beetle
description:
Stag beetle family, genus Dorcus (a subspecies of the flat stag beetle).
*Dorcus titanusu elegans*

A subspecies of the flat stag beetle found in the Amami Islands. It is the most
numerous stag beetle on Amami Oshima. A popular species that grows quite large
in captivity. It gathers at the sap of citrus trees, machilus, chinquapin, and
mallotus trees. In the wild most individuals are under 50mm, and anything over
65mm is quite large. Aim for 70mm+.

name: Amami Lesser Stag Beetle
description:
Stag beetle family, subgenus Dorcus (lesser stag beetles). *Dorcus amamianus*

Although its name means "lesser stag beetle," it resembles the Himeoo stag
beetle in many respects. Its mandibles are short and strongly curved, while its
legs and tarsi are long. Active from late May through October. Less numerous
than the lesser stag beetle found on mainland Japan.

name: Amami Roundwing Stag Beetle
description:
Stag beetle family, genus Neolucanus (roundwing stag beetles).
*Neolucanus protogenetivus*

Active from around September through October, it can be observed deep in
forests dense with giant Castanopsis sieboldii trees. Collecting is prohibited
under the rare wildlife protection ordinances of five municipalities on Amami
Oshima (including its outlying islands) and three towns on Tokunoshima. To
prevent poaching, cameras have been set up in the mountains, and insect patrols
make rounds during the season. Note: simply taking photographs is fine, but if
you need to enter an area that requires a permit, be sure to apply properly.

name: Amami Mountain Stag Beetle
description:
Stag beetle family, genus Lucanus (true stag beetles). *Lucanus ferriei*

Active from around July through September. A rare species found only on Amami
Oshima. Collecting is prohibited by ordinance. Lives in primeval forest above
about 300m elevation. Nocturnal; males can be seen waiting for females high in
trees, but they are hard to spot visually. They are also often seen near the
tops of utility poles. They come to tree sap, fruit traps, and lights, but
collecting them is prohibited.

name: Amami Root Stag Beetle
description:
Stag beetle family, genus Aegus (root stag beetles). *Aegus laevicolis subnitidus*

A subspecies of the root stag beetle found in the Amami Islands, and the
largest-growing of Japan's root stag beetle subspecies. Active from around May
through October. It sometimes comes to the sap of machilus, chinquapin,
mallotus, and Albizia trees. In the wild most individuals are around 20mm, and
28mm is considered large. Aim for 30mm+.

name: Amami Sawtooth Stag Beetle
description:
Stag beetle family, genus Prosopocoilus (sawtooth stag beetles); Amami
subspecies. *Prosopocoilus dissimilis*

Active from mid-June through early September. Among Japan's sawtooth stag
beetles, those from Amami Oshima are especially large, with long, thick,
imposing mandibles. It frequently flies to citrus trees, mallotus, machilus,
chinquapin, ripe Pandanus fruit and banana traps, and streetlights. Most
individuals are around 60mm, and anything over 75mm is large. Aim for 80mm.

name: Amami Deer Stag Beetle
description:
Stag beetle family, genus Rhaetulus (deer stag beetles). *Rhaetulus recticrnis*

Active from around May through September, most easily seen around August.
Collecting is prohibited by ordinance. Areas of relatively higher elevation
offer a better chance of finding it. It is often found on thin branches of
Castanopsis sieboldii or citrus trees. In large individuals the mandibles curve
strongly, like a deer's antlers. Take care not to mistake it for a small
individual of the lesser stag beetle or sawtooth stag beetle and take it home
by accident (never take home an individual you can't identify yourself).

name: Lewis's Horned Stag Beetle
description:
Stag beetle family, subfamily Aesalinae (minute stag beetles), genus Nigidius
(horned gourd stag beetles). *Nigidius lewisi*

Glossy all over the body, with distinctively shaped mandibles, it spends the
whole year inside rotten wood. It can be found year-round in fallen oak and
chinquapin logs and under leaf litter. Telling males and females apart is
difficult. On Amami it has a very localized distribution and rarely comes to
tree sap, making it hard to find.

name: Amami Ridged Flat Stag Beetle
description:
Stag beetle family, subgenus Dorcus (flat stag beetles). *Dorcus metacostatus*

Active from late April through around October, peaking in July. A rare species
endemic to Japan, found only in the Amami Islands, with eight distinct ridges
on its elytra. It frequently flies to citrus trees, machilus, mallotus,
chinquapin, banana traps, and streetlights. Anything over 60mm is large — aim
for 70mm+.
